name: Groq LPU: deterministic single-core-per-token architecture and SRAM-to-DRAM ratio
arithmetic_intensity: The Groq LPU uses a deterministic assembly-line architecture where each token is processed by a single core (SIMD function unit) with no dynamic scheduling, no cache misses, and no variance. All data movement is statically scheduled at compile time. The SRAM-to-DRAM ratio is effectively infinite — there is no DRAM tier. 230 MB of on-chip SRAM at 80 TB/s bandwidth vs GPU HBM at ~8 TB/s. This means the memory hierarchy assumptions are completely inverted: there is no weight streaming from HBM, no cache hierarchy, no prefetching. The compiler must fit the entire model (or a tile of it) in SRAM at compile time.
scales_with: model_size (must fit in 230 MB SRAM per chip, or be tiled across chips)
num_chips (larger models need more chips for capacity)
compile_time (static scheduling means longer compilation for complex models)
workarounds: Tile large models across hundreds of chips (70B-class needs ~300+ chips)
Use the model-independent compiler — no model-specific kernel coding needed
Accept that models larger than 230 MB require multi-chip configurations
Leverage determinism: latency is predictable and holds under load
notes: The architectural point that matters for inference: SRAM-only with no DRAM tier means there is no weight-streaming path. A model larger than 230 MB must be tiled across many chips and the tapeout is fixed at compile time. The compiler statically schedules all data movement and the result is a deterministic assembly line. This is why Groq's headline latency figures hold under load — there is no cache miss variance, no dynamic scheduling overhead. The tradeoff is capacity: 230 MB is small compared to GPU HBM (80-192 GB), so large models need many chips. The 80 TB/s SRAM bandwidth is the key advantage — it eliminates the memory bottleneck that dominates GPU inference.
